title: How it is done
cando: describe processes and services, and understand official notices

about.text: In this lesson you talk about how things are made and how services work, using the passive. You read a product label, a notice at a warehouse gate and a reply that says nothing, and you write a notice of work that will be done. Then you explain how something from your country is made, and chase up a repair that is late.
goals: Say what things are made of and where: They're made of cotton. They're made in our own workshop.
Describe a process step by step with the passive: First, the tea is washed. Then the mint is added.
Talk about the future and rules: It'll be delivered on Thursday. The form must be signed.
Read a product label, a notice and an email, and write a notice of what will be done.
Chase up a repair that has not been done, and get a date and a name.

chapters.title: How is it made?
chapters.text:
In this lesson, you talk about how things are made, and how services work.
First, you listen to Ana. She runs a small café, and she's buying aprons for her staff at a workwear shop. She also wants to collect a jacket she left there for repair.
Listen to how the assistant, Kwame, talks about the aprons. They're made of cotton. They're made here in our own workshop. He doesn't say who makes them. The aprons are more important than the people.
Then listen to the bad news about Ana's jacket: It's still being repaired. And the promise: It'll be finished by Friday.

chapters.title: The passive
chapters.text:
The grammar in this lesson is the passive. We use it when the thing is more important than the person who does the action, or when we don't know who does it.
The passive is be and a past participle. Cotton is grown in Egypt. The aprons are made here.
For the past, use was or were. The parcel was delivered yesterday.
For something happening now, use being. My jacket is being repaired.
For the future, use will be. The aprons will be delivered on Thursday.
After must, should and can, use be. The form must be signed. It can't be repaired.
Don't forget the small word be. Not: the form must signed. Say: the form must be signed.
If the person is important, add by. This chair was made by my grandfather.

chapters.title: A label, a notice and a reply
chapters.text:
Next, you read three short texts.
The first is a label from a work jacket. It tells you what the jacket is made of, where it was made, and how to wash it.
The second is a notice at a warehouse gate. Notices use the passive a lot. Deliveries are accepted at Gate 2. The road will be inspected.
The third is an email reply to a complaint. Every sentence is polite. But look again. It gives no date, no name and no number. It's a reply that says nothing.
Then you write a notice of your own. Say what will be done, when, and who to contact.

chapters.title: How it's made, and where's my repair?
chapters.text:
The task has two parts.
First, a colleague asks about something from your country: a food, a drink, a cloth or a craft. Explain how it's made, step by step. First, the tea is washed. Then the mint is added.
Then you phone a repair shop. You left something there three weeks ago, and it still isn't ready. Chase it up. Be polite, but don't accept a reply that says nothing. Ask for a date and a name.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a story or an article from the Library about how something is made or done.
Read it once for the main idea. Then read it again, and notice the steps in the process.

warmup.prompt: Look at the label in your shirt or your shoes. Where were they made?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Many things we use every day travel a long way before we buy them. In this lesson, you talk about how things are made, where, and by whom.

conversation.title: How is it made?
conversation.setting: Ana runs a small café. She goes to Calder & Finch, a workwear shop, to buy aprons for her staff and to collect a jacket she left there for repair.
lines: Good morning. Can I help you?
Hi. I'm looking for aprons for my café staff. Something strong that washes well.
These are very popular. They're made of cotton, with steel buttons, and they're made here in our own workshop.
Oh, really? Where does the cotton come from?
It's grown in Egypt, and the fabric is imported from there. The cutting and the sewing are done here.
Great. I need eight. Are they in stock?
We've only got five in stock at the moment. The other three will be delivered from our warehouse on Thursday.
That's fine. Can I track the delivery?
Yes. A tracking number will be sent to you by email.
Perfect. Oh, and I left a jacket here for repair two weeks ago. Is it ready?
Let me check. I'm sorry, it's still being repaired. A new zip had to be ordered.
Two weeks is a long time. When will it be ready?
It'll be finished by Friday. I'll chase it up with the workshop today.
Thank you. Could you call me as soon as it's done?

questions.why: Kwame says: They're made here in our own workshop.

questions.q: When will the other three aprons be delivered?
questions.why: Kwame says: The other three will be delivered from our warehouse on Thursday.

questions.a: It's still being repaired, because a new zip was needed.
wrong: It was sent to Egypt by mistake.
questions.why: Kwame says: It's still being repaired. A new zip had to be ordered.

items.meaning: To make things in large numbers, using machines, usually in a factory.
items.example: The company manufactures shoes, and most of them are sold abroad.

items.meaning: To send goods to another country, to sell them there.
items.example: Kenya exports tea all over the world.

items.meaning: To bring goods into a country from another country, to sell or use them.
items.example: We import most of our fruit in the winter.

items.meaning: All the companies that make one kind of product or give one kind of service.
items.example: The clothing industry employs thousands of people in this city.

items.meaning: A series of steps that you follow to make or do something.
items.example: Making cheese is a slow process.

items.meaning: In its natural state, before it is cooked or changed in a factory.
items.example: Raw cotton is white and soft, like a cloud.

items.meaning: A light, natural material from a plant. Many shirts and towels are made of it.
items.example: This shirt is 100% cotton.

items.meaning: Thick, warm material made from the hair of sheep.
items.example: My winter jumper is made of wool.

items.meaning: A strong material that bends and doesn't let water through. Tyres and boots are made of it.
items.example: Work boots often have rubber soles.

items.meaning: A very strong, hard metal. Bridges, tools and cars are made of it.
items.example: The gate is made of steel.

items.meaning: A room or a building where things are made or repaired, by hand or with small machines.
items.example: My uncle repairs furniture in a workshop behind his house.

items.meaning: A large building where goods are kept before they are sent to shops or customers.
items.example: The orders are packed in the warehouse and sent out the same day.

items.meaning: Available in a shop now, ready to buy.
items.example: Sorry, that size isn't in stock at the moment.

items.meaning: To follow where something is, for example a parcel, using a number or an app.
items.example: You can track your parcel online.

items.meaning: To contact someone again, to ask about something that is late.
items.example: I'll chase up the repair with the workshop today.

sound.title: Small words in the passive
sound.explain: In the passive, the small words in the middle are quick and quiet: is, are, was, being, will be. The main verb is strong and clear. But don't drop the small words, because a listener still needs them. Listen to each group, then say it.
groups: it's made · they're made · it was made
it's being repaired · it'll be delivered · it must be signed
lines: They're made here in our own workshop.
I'm sorry, it's still being repaired.

sayIt.instructions: Say Kwame's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Can you hear the small words: are, will be, being?
lines: These are very popular. They're made of cotton, with steel buttons, and they're made here in our own workshop.
We've only got five in stock at the moment. The other three will be delivered from our warehouse on Thursday.
Let me check. I'm sorry, it's still being repaired. A new zip had to be ordered.
It'll be finished by Friday. I'll chase it up with the workshop today.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. None of them says who does the action.
examples: They're made here in our own workshop.
The other three will be delivered from our warehouse on Thursday.
A tracking number will be sent to you by email.
I'm sorry, it's still being repaired.
spot.question: Who makes the aprons, delivers them and repairs the jacket? Why doesn't Kwame say? What comes after are, will be and being?
spot.answer: We don't know exactly who, and it isn't important: the aprons and the jacket are what matter to Ana. That's why Kwame uses the passive. After are, will be and being comes the past participle: made, delivered, sent, repaired.

rules.title: The passive: it's made, it was delivered, it's being repaired
rule: be + past participle, when the thing matters more than the person: The aprons are made here.
Facts and processes: Cotton is grown in Egypt. The fabric is cut by hand.
The past: The boxes were delivered on Monday. The bridge was built in 1885.
Happening now: My jacket is being repaired. The lift is being checked.
Add by only when the person matters: This chair was made by my grandfather.
rules.mistake: Not: The aprons are make here. Not: The parcel delivered yesterday. Say: The aprons are made here. The parcel was delivered yesterday.

rules.title: The future and rules: it'll be done, it must be signed
rule: will be + past participle: Your order will be delivered on Thursday.
must, should or can + be + past participle: This form must be signed.
Negative: Bags must not be left here. It can't be repaired.
Questions: When will it be ready? Can it be repaired?
Notices use it a lot: The main gate will be closed from 3 to 5 June.
rules.mistake: Not: The form must signed. Say: The form must be signed.

practice.why: The shoes don't make anything: they are made.

practice.q: My car ___ at the moment, so I'm taking the bus.
practice.why: The work is happening now, so we use is being + past participle.

practice.q: The parcel ___ yesterday, but nobody was at home.
practice.why: It happened yesterday, so we use the past passive: was delivered.

practice.q: Your new sofa will ___ on Thursday.
practice.why: The future passive is will be + past participle.

practice.q: This form must ___ by your manager.
practice.why: After must, the passive needs be: must be signed.

practice.q: All visitors' bags ___ at the gate.
practice.why: The bags don't check anything: they are checked.

practice.q: The lift is out of order. It ___ tomorrow morning.
practice.why: The future passive is will be + past participle.

practice.q: Smoking ___ allowed anywhere in the building.
practice.why: The passive negative is is not + past participle.

practice.q: Most of the tea we drink ___ from India and Kenya.
practice.why: The tea doesn't import anything: it is imported.

practice.q: These chairs were made ___ a local carpenter.
practice.why: By tells you the person who did the action.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose something you use every day: a mug, a pair of shoes, a phone or a loaf of bread. Write four sentences about it with the passive: what it is made of, where it was made, how you got it, and one thing that must be done to it.
yourTurn.model: My work boots are made of leather and rubber. They were made in Portugal and sold in a shop near my flat. They were delivered to my door in a paper bag. They must be cleaned every week, or the leather gets hard.

text.title: A label, a gate notice and a reply
text.body:
PRACTICE LABEL: this product does not exist.
CALDER & FINCH · WORK JACKET
Outer fabric: 100% cotton. Lining: wool. Buttons: steel.
Made in our workshop in Leeds, UK.
Packaging: made from recycled paper. Please recycle it.
Suitable for indoor and outdoor work.
Wash at 30°C. Do not iron the badge.
Free repairs for one year. Bring the jacket and this label.

- - - - - - - -

PRACTICE NOTICE: this warehouse does not exist.
CALDER & FINCH WAREHOUSE · NOTICE AT THE GATE
All visitors must sign in at the security office.
Vehicles must not be left at the gate.
Deliveries are accepted at Gate 2 only, from 7 am to 4 pm.
Forklifts may only be operated by trained staff.
MAINTENANCE WORK: The main gate will be closed from 3 to 5 June. Repairs will be carried out, and the road will be inspected. Please use Gate 2.

- - - - - - - -

From: Facilities Team
To: Omar Haddad
Subject: RE: Broken door at the staff entrance
Dear Mr Haddad,
Thank you for your email. Your report has been received, and the matter is being investigated. The door will be inspected in due course, and any necessary work will be carried out as soon as possible. You will be contacted when a decision has been made.
Kind regards,
Facilities Team

gist.q: Which text is a reply that says nothing?
gist.why: The email gives no date, no name and no number, so Mr Haddad still doesn't know what will happen.

gist.q: Who is the notice at the gate for?
gist.a: visitors, drivers and staff at the warehouse
gist.why: It gives rules for visitors, vehicles, deliveries and staff.

detail.q: What is the lining of the jacket made of?
What should you do with the jacket's packaging?
wrong: bring it back with the jacket
detail.why: The label says: Packaging: made from recycled paper. Please recycle it.

detail.q: You're delivering boxes on 4 June. Which gate do you use?
detail.why: Deliveries are accepted at Gate 2 only, and the main gate is closed from 3 to 5 June.

detail.q: When will Mr Haddad's door be inspected?
detail.why: In due course means at some time in the future, with no date.

items.meaning: To try to find out the facts about something, for example a problem or an accident.
items.example: The company is investigating the cause of the fire.

items.meaning: To look at something carefully, to check that it is safe or correct.
items.example: An engineer will inspect the lift tomorrow.

items.meaning: To do a piece of work, a task or a plan.
items.example: The repairs will be carried out next week.

items.meaning: The work of checking and repairing things, so that they stay in good condition.
items.example: The pool is closed for maintenance on Mondays.

items.meaning: A machine that carries people or goods, for example a car, a van or a lorry.
items.example: No vehicles are allowed past this gate.

items.meaning: To write your name, or scan a card, when you arrive at a building.
items.example: All visitors must sign in at reception.

items.meaning: To use and control a machine.
items.example: Only trained staff can operate the forklift.

items.meaning: To treat used things, like paper, glass or plastic, so that they can be used again.
items.example: We recycle all our cardboard boxes.

items.meaning: The box, paper or plastic that a product is sold in.
items.example: Too much packaging goes straight in the bin.

items.meaning: Right for a particular person, purpose or situation.
items.example: These boots are suitable for outdoor work.

items.meaning: Material made from cotton, wool or other threads, used for clothes and curtains.
items.example: The fabric is cut into pieces, and then the pieces are sewn together.

write.task: Write a notice for your workplace, your building or a club. Something will be repaired, cleaned or changed. Say what will be done and when, what people must do, and who to contact. Make sure your notice says something: a date, a time and a name.
checklist: I said what will be done, with will be + a past participle.
I gave a date and a time.
I wrote one rule with must be or must not be.
I gave a name or a number to contact.

card.title: How it's made, and where's my repair?
card.situation: A new colleague asks you about something from your country: a food, a drink, a cloth or a craft. Later, you phone a repair shop. Three weeks ago you left your laptop there, and they promised it would be ready in a week. You still haven't heard anything.
card.goal: Explain how the thing is made, step by step, with the passive. Then phone the shop and chase up your repair. Don't finish the call until you have a date and a name.

phrases: I'm calling to chase up a repair.
I left it with you on … . The reference number is … .
I'm sorry, but soon isn't a date. When exactly will it be ready?
prepare.notes: Make notes for both parts. Part 1: the thing, what it is made from, and three or four steps in order. Part 2: what you left, when, your reference number, and what you want: a date and a name.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, explain how your thing is made to a partner, and answer two questions about it. Then your teacher is the repair shop assistant, who gives vague answers at first. Chase up your repair until you get a date and a name.
doIt.wehel: First, you are my new colleague. Ask me how something from my country is made, and ask me two questions about it. Then you are an assistant at a repair shop. I left my laptop with you three weeks ago, and it isn't ready. At first, give me vague answers, like: It's being looked at. When I ask politely for a date and a name, give them to me. Use clear, simple English.

model.title: Mint tea, and a late repair
lines: What's that you're drinking? It smells lovely.
Mint tea. It's very popular in Morocco, where I'm from.
It's made with green tea, fresh mint and sugar. First, the tea is washed with a little hot water. Then the mint and the sugar are added.
Almost. It's poured from high above the glass, so it gets a little foam on top. It's usually drunk with friends.
Hello. I'm calling to chase up a repair. I left my laptop with you three weeks ago, and I was told it would be ready in a week.
Let me look. Can I have your reference number, please?
Ah, yes. It's being looked at. It'll be done soon.
I'm sorry, but soon isn't a date. When exactly will it be ready, and who is working on it?
I do apologise. A new part has been ordered. It'll be fitted on Thursday, and Omar will call you by five o'clock.
Thursday, by five o'clock, and Omar will call. Thank you.
compare: Did you explain the process step by step: First, it's …; then it's …?
Did you use the passive: it's made, it's added, it's served?
Did you say when you left the item, and give your reference number?
Did you ask for a date and a name, and say them back to check?

canDo: I can say what something is made of and where it is made.
I can explain a process step by step with the passive.
I can understand a product label and an official notice.
I can tell a reply that says nothing from one that gives real information.
I can chase up a repair and get a date and a name.

reading.before: Look at the title and the pictures. What is being made or done in this story or article?
reading.talk: What was the most interesting step in the process? Explain it to Wehel in four sentences with the passive: First, it's …; then it's …

quiz.q: These boots ___ of leather and rubber.
quiz.why: The boots don't make anything: they are made.

quiz.q: Your order ___ on Friday. You'll get a text.
quiz.why: The future passive is will be + past participle.

quiz.q: Sorry, you can't use the lift. It ___ .
quiz.why: The work is happening now, so we use is being repaired.

quiz.q: This form must ___ before you start work.
quiz.why: After must, the passive needs be: must be signed.

quiz.q: A large building where goods are kept before they go to shops is a ___ .
quiz.why: Goods are kept in a warehouse; things are made or repaired in a workshop.

quiz.q: My order is two weeks late. I'm going to phone the shop and ___ it up.
quiz.why: To chase something up is to ask again about something that is late.

quiz.q: Please don't put these boxes in the bin. We ___ all our packaging.
quiz.why: To recycle is to treat used things so that they can be used again.

quiz.q: I've lost the bag ___ my sister gave me.
quiz.why: That is for things: the bag that my sister gave me.

quiz.q: When I arrived at the party, most people ___ .
quiz.why: They left before I arrived, so we use the past perfect.

quiz.q: If it ___ tomorrow, we'll stay at home.
quiz.why: There is no will after if: if it rains.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the workwear shop conversation in pairs. Then learners pick things around them and ask each other: What's it made of? Where was it made? Is it in stock?

Day 2: a process chain. In small groups, learners describe how something is made or done (bread, a cup of coffee, sending a parcel), one passive sentence each. Then read the three texts together and talk about why the reply says nothing.

Day 3: the task. Each learner explains how something from their country is made. Then you are the repair shop assistant: give vague passive answers until the learner politely asks for a date and a name.
Day 4: talk about the book or article and its process. Learners read their notices aloud, and the class checks each one for a date, a rule and a name to contact.
